https://www.rferl.org/a/shanghai-securit.body: Features 'Shanghai' Grouping At 25: Rifts, Rivalries, And A Show Of Unity By Zamira Eshanova and RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service August 31, 2026 21:12 CET 'Shanghai' Grouping At 25: Rifts, Rivalries, And A Show Of Unity Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on August 31 on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek. With a summit in Bishkek, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) is turning 25 at a moment of extraordinary tension that touches directly on many of the increasingly sprawling regional group's members. Iran is at war with the United States, Russia's war on Ukraine continues to rage with no sign of a let-up, China faces mounting US pressure over trade, and nuclear-armed foes India and Pakistan sit together despite deep rivalry, just to name a few. The four Central Asian members -- host country Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan -- are regional players but also the objects of various nations seeking to increase their sway, including China, Russia, India, and the United States, which is not a member of the SCO. SEE ALSO: Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit In an interview with the People's Daily, the newspaper of the Central Committee of China's Communist Party, SCO Secretary-General Nurlan Yermekbaev of Kazakhstan touted the "Shanghai spirit," which he said involves mutual trust, respect, and benefit, among other qualities he asserted make the group appealing to the so-called Global South. But behind these "shared values" are deep differences, with members using the SCO platform to pursue their own, often competing agendas. Each member "has its own distinct position, and the major powers have views that differ from one another," Kyrgyz political analyst Emil Juraev said. China and India "have differing positions on many issues, and there are also areas of dispute between them," Juraev said. "Russia is trying to exert influence on the world and...continues its war without stopping it. In addition, there is Iran. Everyone is waiting to see what Iran will do." Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Bishkek on August 31. The 26th annual SCO summit marks 25 years since it was established by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. India, Pakistan, Iran, and Belarus are now members, and along with observer states and dialogue partners it represents nearly half of the world's population and roughly a quarter of the global economy. "Bishkek has become a world capital today," a local paper proclaimed on August 31 as leaders gathered for bilateral meetings on the eve of the formal summit. The September 1 meeting is expected to produce a Bishkek Declaration marking the anniversary along with thematic statements and decisions covering security, the economy, transport, environmental protection, artificial intelligence, and cultural and humanitarian cooperation. Past gatherings have produced no momentous decisions, however, and for members large and small it may be more about show than substance. Despite deep differences within the organization, the SCO gives its members and observers a platform to appear together on the international stage and project the weight of a larger collective, said Reid Standish, a nonresident research fellow at the Central European Institute of Asian Studies and a former RFE/RL correspondent. "It may not have major policy achievements to its name and it can be hamstrung by its internal rivalries, but the SCO still clearly serves a purpose in bringing these leaders together in a forum that isn't dominated by Western powers," he said. "The SCO's leaders clearly attach meaning to this, otherwise they would not be attending." China is the SCO's most influential member, and its economic weight has put Beijing at the center of mounting international pressure over trade. SEE ALSO: What If China Doesn't Play Ball? US Sanctions Campaign Faces Its Biggest Test Ahead of an August 31 meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors halfway around the world in Asheville, North Carolina, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he would encourage members to rethink their trade with China, calling Beijing's roughly $1.2 trillion global trade surplus unsustainable. Last week, Bessent urged countries to cut ties with Iran as part of an effort to " sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone." For Iran, the signal it hopes the SCO summit will send is that it is not alone. "In the confrontation between Iran and America, we should expect stronger statements here, statements about Western influence and pressure or a declaration expressing disagreement with the processes in Iran or saying something along the lines of, 'You are doing the wrong thing,'" Kyrgyz political analyst Chynara Esengul said. Likewise Russia, which is under increasingly tight Western sanctions over its war against Ukraine. In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin on suspicion of war crimes over the illegal transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia. For China, Standish said, SCO meetings "serve a useful purpose in providing important optics to the world that key global decisions can be reached without the presence of Western leaders." https://www.rferl.org/a/armenia-tripp-tr.body: Armenia Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape By Zamira Eshanova and RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service September 06, 2026 13:34 CET Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian speaks at an SCO summit in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, on September 1. Armenia is courting Central Asia as it intensifies efforts to break ground on an ambitious trade corridor named after US President Donald Trump -- the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP. Part of a peace deal between Yerevan and Baku, the planned corridor would run across Armenian territory, linking Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave while opening a new east-west trade artery bypassing Russia and Iran. The proposed plan has the backing of Washington, but has riled Moscow and Tehran, two countries under heavy Western sanctions. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian has in recent weeks pushed for the involvement of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. But both countries, observers say, are wary of angering Russia, a key political and economic player in Central Asia. Pashinian discussed TRIPP with the leaders of Azerbaijan and India as well representatives from the United States during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek on September 1. SEE ALSO: Bypassing The Kremlin: Armenia And Azerbaijan Expand Trade, Testing Russia's Grip On August 27, Pashinian confirmed to RFE/RL’s Armenian Service that he had discussed Kazakhstan’s possible participation in TRIPP during a recent phone call with Kazkah President Qasym-Zhomart Tokaev. “We discussed this issue in relation to Kazakhstan and the TRIPP project. Various countries are now showing interest,” Pashinian said, without elaborating. Kyrgyz official Daniyar Amangeldiev told RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service that the government had yet to receive an official proposal. Public Rollout While the participation of potential regional partners remains uncertain, Armenia and the United States are moving ahead with plans to publicly launch the project. On September 1, they launched the official TRIPP Armenia Facebook page , jointly managed by the Armenian Foreign Ministry and US Embassy in Yerevan. On the same day, US and Armenian officials met in Armenia’s province of Syunik, where the 43-kilometer-long corridor is planned, to discuss the project and its potential economic benefits. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian (left) meets with US President Donald Trump in Egypt in late 2025. The United States owns 74 percent of the project, with Armenia retaining the rest. Washington has committed an initial $145 million. Pashinian has called TRIPP a “multibillion-dollar project.” TRIPP was approved by the Armenian government in July. The Constitutional Court is expected to rule on it on September 15 before it goes to parliament for a final vote. Washington has pledged to help secure additional financing from public and private investors, although no new investors or funds have been announced. For landlocked Armenia, the project is seen as a way to end its economic isolation and become a regional transport hub. SEE ALSO: Armenia Wants In On Asia-Europe Trade. Russian Rail Control Stands In The Way. Unveiled as part of the US-mediated peace process following Armenia's war with Azerbaijan over its breakaway region of Nagorno-Karabakh, TRIPP envisages rail and road infrastructure, possible oil and gas pipelines, and fiber-optic and electricity ventures. Since Azerbaijan regained control over Karabakh in a lightening offensive in September 2023, Armenia has shifted its geopolitical orientation, distancing itself from longtime ally Moscow and aligning more closely with the West. Bishkek, Astana 'Curiously Muted' Kazakhstan has publicly expressed interest in participating in TRIPP. TRIPP would complement the Middle Corridor, an emerging 6,500-kilometer-long trade route, bypassing Russia, that connects China to Europe through Central Asia and the Caucasus. TRIPP would provide onward connectivity from Azerbaijan through Armenia and Nakhchivan to Turkey and Europe. Kyrgyz officials have also presented TRIPP as a potential extension of the country’s transport links to Europe. “Our railway would reach Baku, which would also open a direct route for us to Turkey... It is a new opportunity,” Kyrgyzstan’s ambassador to the United States, Edil Baisalov, told RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service. Still, neither Bishkek nor Astana has publicly committed to participating in TRIPP. Kyrgyz political analyst Emilbek Dzhuraev said both countries have been “curiously muted.” SEE ALSO: Russia Uses Economic Chokehold To Counter Armenia's Westward Tilt “While both of them have had positive exchanges with the US, their SCO partners -- Iran in particular, but also Russia -- do not welcome TRIPP, and therefore, probably, they are hesitant at jumping on this opportunity,” Dzhuraev said. Russia, he added, may be the biggest factor behind their caution, given Moscow’s increasingly tense relations with Pashinian’s government. “Russia has a still greater stake in this -- given its collapsing hold on Armenia -- and hence, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan would not be cheered on by Russia to join TRIPP,” he said. https://www.rferl.org/a/kazakhstan-elect.body: News Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote By Zamira Eshanova August 24, 2026 17:36 CET Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Members of a local electoral commission count ballots at a polling station during parliamentary elections in Almaty, southeastern Kazakhstan, on August 23. Four months ago, the Adilet party did not exist. Today, it dominates Kazakhstan’s political landscape, following an election in which it gained 71.17 percent of the vote according to results announced on August 24. The vote marks a further tightening of President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev's grip on power -- and was roundly criticized by international election observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). “The 23 August early parliamentary elections, while technically well prepared, took place in an environment lacking political pluralism. Political choice was reduced by the lack of distinct political alternatives, with all contesting parties supporting the incumbent President’s policies,” an OSCE statement said. In the August 24 statement , issued a day after the vote itself, the OSCE reported misuse of public resources, including public-sector employees being mobilized to attend campaign events, and concluded that Adilet had "an undue advantage that blurred the line between state and party.” The OSCE noted that independent candidates had been excluded from the election, a factor which “limited political participation and electoral competitiveness.” Observers also cast doubt on the results themselves, stating that discrepancies between what they saw at polling stations and official turnout data “raised questions about the integrity of the voter turnout reporting and the counting process.” OSCE missions have made similar criticisms of all previous elections held in Kazakhstan since it became independent after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, noting a lack of genuine political competition in an authoritarian country dominated for decades by presidents Nursultan Nazarbaev (1991-2019) and his successor, Toqaev. SEE ALSO: Kazakh Voters Appear To Approve Controversial Changes That Critics Say May Concentrate President's Power When Adilet was formed, in April, it absorbed the ruling party that had dominated Kazakhstan during and since the Nazarbaev era. Its stated aim is to implement Toqaev's policies and it will now comfortably control Kazakhstan's new unicameral parliament, the Kurultai. Adilet’s vote share was more than eleven times that of its nearest rival. The election was the first since constitutional changes rammed through by Toqaev earlier this year to switch from a previous bicameral structure. Media Pressure Before the Vote The election took place amid reports of pressure on independent activists and media. Almaty-based civil activist Asset Abishev said police blocked access to his home on August 23, which he described as interference with his right to vote. Another activist, Nurbol Arterkhan, who is under probation and subject to electronic monitoring, said he was repeatedly required to report to probation officials on election day and that police later visited his home. SEE ALSO: Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, five prominent journalists have been jailed or convicted since mid-July, while criminal cases have been opened against two others. Several have also been barred from practicing journalism. Media freedom was another major concern in the OSCE assessment. “Long-standing concerns about arrests and pressure on independent journalists generate pervasive self-censorship,” it noted in its statement. Sevilay Celenk, who headed a team of observers from the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), also raised the issue. “Without an inclusive, credible, and pluralistic media environment, political participation and representation are fundamentally limited, especially during elections,” Celenk said. Key Takeaways Oil prices surged to a four-month high on September 11 amid fears of prolonged supply disruptions and renewed inflation. US President Donald Trump said he had no regrets about going to war with Iran despite the conflict's potential impact on November's midterm elections Gulf Arab foreign ministers are expected to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi in Oman next week as regional powers seek support for a temporary arrangement to restore commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian arrived in New Delhi on September 11 for a BRICS summit, with the escalating Middle East conflict expected to feature prominently. Several US military aircraft were damaged in Iranian missile strikes on a base in Jordan housing American soldiers, according to reports. New posts 14:24 Houthis Reach Strategic Island On Key Red Sea Shipping Route Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels have reached the strategic island of Perim, also known as Mayyun, in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, potentially strengthening their grip on one of the world's most important shipping routes, according to Yemeni government sources. Four government sources told Reuters on September 11 that Houthi forces had reached the island, while the German dpa news agency cited a Yemeni government source as saying the group had taken control of it. Reuters reported that forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized government had withdrawn from Perim. AFP cited an unnamed Yemeni military official as saying the Houthis now control the country's entire Red Sea coast. All territory that had been under government control "on the western coast has fallen" following the Houthis' seizure of Perim and the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, AFP quoted the military official as saying. Perim, or Mayyun, sits at the southern entrance to the Bab al-Mandab, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a crucial route for trade and energy shipments between Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal. The waterway's strategic importance has grown sharply since the Iran war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, another of the world's key energy chokepoints. The Houthi advance follows the group's reported capture of the Red Sea port of Mocha on September 10. Government sources also reported Houthi advances on the mainland and other islands in the strait. The developments raise the prospect of disruptions to shipping through the Red Sea at a time when Saudi Arabia has become increasingly reliant on the route for oil exports because of conflict-related restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz. Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share 11:54 Iranian President Arrives In New Delhi For BRICS Summit Amid Gulf Crisis Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian (center right) arrives to attend a BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 11. Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian arrived in the Indian capital, New Delhi, on September 11 to join the leaders of BRICS countries for a summit, with the escalating Middle East conflict expected to feature prominently on the agenda. BRICS, a grouping of major emerging markets and developing countries, takes its name from Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It expanded from five to 11 members in 2024 and 2025, adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Making his first visit to India since taking office in 2024, Pezeshkian is scheduled to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Iran's IRNA state news agency reported. The two-day BRICS Leaders' Summit begins on September 12 and is expected to bring together Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, among other leaders. Iran, which joined BRICS in 2024, is directly involved in the conflict, while fellow member the UAE has faced Iranian missile attacks and taken measures against Tehran. The UAE suspended all trade and financial transactions with Iran in August following the attacks, underscoring growing tensions within BRICS as the summit convenes amid the deepening regional crisis. The UAE is expected to be represented by Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. With reporting by AFP and Reuters Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share 09:14 Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount Oil prices surged to a four-month high on September 11 as escalating threats to two of the world's key energy shipping routes fueled fears of prolonged supply disruptions and renewed inflation. Brent crude touched $109.97 a barrel after jumping more than 6 percent a day earlier, before falling back. The benchmark was still on track for a weekly price gain of about 11 percent. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain restricted as the United States and Iran trade attacks, while the reported seizure of Yemen's Red Sea port of Mocha by Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has raised concerns over shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The oil rally intensified inflation concerns across global markets, pushing government bond yields sharply higher as investors increased bets on further interest-rate hikes. JPMorgan analysts now expect eight of nine developed-market central banks to raise interest rates by the end of the year as policymakers contend with persistent inflation and rising commodity prices. With reporting by Reuters Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share 08:18 Gulf States, Iran Plan Talks On Hormuz Shipping Deal, FT Reports Foreign ministers from Persian Gulf Arab states are expected to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi in Oman next week as regional powers seek support for a temporary arrangement to restore commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reported . The meeting, an Omani initiative, is scheduled for September 14 in the coastal city of Salalah, according to two people briefed on the matter cited by the FT. One of the people said details were still being finalized, but that a number of states had confirmed their participation and the meeting was expected to go ahead. Oman and Iran have been negotiating a temporary arrangement under which ships would enter the strait through Iranian waters and mostly exit through Omani territory. Diplomats cautioned, however, that a US-Iran agreement would ultimately be needed for the waterway to fully reopen. One person briefed on the talks told the FT that Iran and Oman hoped to get GCC backing and use it to press Washington to lift its blockade of Iranian ports. Gulf states, meanwhile, want to ensure that any arrangement is temporary and allows vessels to enter and leave. The diplomatic push comes after a short-lived US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June unraveled amid disputes over shipping through Hormuz. Washington has told mediators it wants any new agreement to also address Iran's nuclear program, while Tehran is demanding concessions including an end to the blockade and permission to resume oil

https://www.rferl.org/a/iran-infiltratio.body: Iran 'Infiltration' Bill Exposes Iran's Internal Divisions Over Wartime Security Crackdown By Kian Sharifi September 10, 2026 15:43 CET 'Infiltration' Bill Exposes Iran's Internal Divisions Over Wartime Security Crackdown Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf speaks during an event marking 40 days since the burial of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in Karbala, Iraq, on August 20. Iran's parliament is trying to turn fears of foreign infiltration into law. But as lawmakers work through the legislation, the debate is exposing an increasingly awkward question for the Islamic republic: How far should the state go in policing Iranians' contact with the outside world? At the center of that debate is Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who, at least publicly, is doing a balancing act. He has defended the need for tougher measures against foreign infiltration while warning that the current draft of the legislation goes too far. "No patriot opposes countering foreign infiltration," Qalibaf said during a recent parliamentary session. But, he added, lawmakers needed to ensure that people's "rights, their lives, and their trade" were not affected. SEE ALSO: Iran Parliament Advances Bill Criminalizing Contact With Foreign Media and Institutions He said security agencies may need to be able to vet Iranians' contacts with foreigners but that they cannot demand permission at every stage. "They say they want to be certain, to have permission sought from them at every stage," the conservative speaker said. "That's not possible, because then we'd have to lock the country down." That balancing act gets to the heart of a bill that was conceived as a wartime response to genuine security failures. The two recent wars exposed how deeply Israeli intelligence had penetrated Iran and prompted calls for tougher measures to identify and prevent foreign influence. But what began as a security response has evolved into a much broader fight over the boundaries of the Islamic republic's security state. The bill, formally called the Plan To Counter The Infiltration Of Intelligence Services And Foreign Governments Or Institutions but commonly referred to as the "infiltration bill," would require Iranians to obtain prior approval from the Intelligence Ministry and the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Intelligence Organization before engaging in a sweeping range of activities. Those activities include publishing books or articles, academic cooperation, interviews with foreign media deemed "hostile," and participation in scientific conferences or arts festivals. The bill also includes provisions criminalizing interviews, discussions, and other communication with media deemed hostile, as well as sending photographs, videos, audio, or other material to foreign media, with violations punishable by prison terms of up to two years. Parliament approved the bill's general framework in mid-August by a lopsided 183-4 vote. The draft has since expanded from 19 to 33 articles as it has moved through the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee. Only its first two articles have so far cleared the floor, while the remaining provisions remain subject to revision. Even if parliament approves them, the bill will still require Guardian Council approval before it can become law. The political resistance, however, has already begun. SEE ALSO: Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount Qalibaf has sent two of the bill's most consequential provisions -- Articles 7 and 8, which deal with the disclosure process and penalties for exceeding the scope of a permit -- back to the committee because of ambiguities. Qalibaf has insisted that parliament must address the security agencies' concerns, saying their "needs" would be met "within reasonable bounds." But he has rejected the idea that the Intelligence Ministry and IRGC Intelligence Organization should effectively have the power to approve Iranians' foreign contacts at every turn. He has also dismissed suggestions that the bill should be shelved at the government's request. When First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref claimed Qalibaf had privately promised to stop the legislation, an MP repeated the allegation on the parliamentary floor. Qalibaf rejected it, stressing that parliament is not "a branch of the government." The result is a political fault line that does not fit neatly into Iran's usual hardliner-versus-reformist divide. Some lawmakers have been far more openly hostile to the bill. Mohammad Mehdi Shahriari, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, called it "completely at odds with national interests." The government of President Masud Pezeshkian has also publicly opposed the bill. Hossein Afshin, the vice president for science, technology, and the knowledge-based economy, warned the current draft could isolate Iran's academic and research community and lead to "scientific stagnation." He pointed to the risks of an accelerated brain drain and additional obstacles for Iranian scientists working or studying abroad. Conservative commentator Mohammad Mohajeri, editor of Khabar Online, made much the same point more sarcastically, writing on X that just as the government was trying to persuade Iranians living abroad to return home, parliament was giving elites, scholars, and students fresh reasons to leave. The controversy has also attracted international criticism. On September 3, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran called for the bill to be withdrawn, warning it could further restrict fundamental freedoms and isolate Iranians from the international community. UN Special Rapporteur on Iran Mai Sato separately warned that Iranian intelligence agencies should not become "the gatekeepers of Iranian people's contact with the world." For Iran's political establishment, however, the more immediate problem may be closer to home. Few in the system appear willing to dispute that foreign infiltration is a genuine security threat. The argument is increasingly over what should follow from that threat and where the state should draw the line. https://uhrp.org/report/manifest-risk-ne.body: Manifest Risk: New “Air Silk Road” Cargo Flights Carry Risk of Uyghur Forced Labor into Europe - Uyghur Human Rights Project Skip to content Manifest Risk: New “Air Silk Road” Cargo Flights Carry Risk of Uyghur Forced Labor into Europe July 31, 2025 Table of Contents A Uyghur Human Rights Project report by Peter Irwin and Dr. Henryk Szadziewski. Read our press statement on the briefing, download the full briefing in English , and read a printable, one-page summary of the report. Read coverage and citations of the report in Politico (cited again in April 2026), The Daily Mail , Ecotextile News , Business and Human Rights Resource Centre , Center for Strategic International Studies (CSIS) , The Loadstar , Devidiscourse , Pulse , Domino Theory , Freight News , and ANI News . I. Key Takeaways Air cargo routes are rapidly expanding between Ürümchi and over a dozen European cities. Since June 2024, nine cargo companies have launched new air freight routes between Ürümchi and cities across the EU, UK, and Switzerland, creating a direct trade corridor from a region where the Chinese government is perpetrating genocide and atrocity crimes, including forced labor. Goods transported by air include products from sectors linked to Uyghur forced labor. Cargo includes e-commerce goods, textiles, footwear, electronics, and agricultural products, sectors documented as tainted by Uyghur forced labor. New air freight routes are part of China’s broader Air Silk Road strategy to integrate the Uyghur Region into global markets. The Chinese government has positioned Ürümchi as a central hub for transcontinental cargo flights under the Belt and Road Initiative. Immediate action is required to close enforcement gaps and prevent complicity. Without urgent intervention, the growing volume of cargo flights risks embedding Uyghur forced labor into European supply chains. The European Union and national authorities must act to inspect high-risk cargo, allocate enforcement resources, and uphold commitments to end forced labor imports. II. A Rapid Rise in Air Cargo Links Between Ürümchi and Europe On May 21, a cargo flight carrying over 50 tonnes of e-commerce goods from Ürümchi landed in Tallinn, Estonia after making a short stop in Tashkent, Uzbekistan. The route, the first of its kind, offers EU importers a streamlined channel for sourcing goods from a region where the Chinese government is perpetrating atrocities, including systemic state-imposed forced labor. According to a new UHRP analysis of cargo flight traffic from June 2024 to May 2025, nine cargo carriers operated at least 20 direct or indirect 1 In this report, “indirect” refers to routes with one stopover. routes transporting goods from Ürümchi to destinations across the European Union, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom—including the newly established route to Tallinn. 2 See Table 1 for full data on the number of flights and destinations. Historical cargo flight data shows the emergence of entirely new direct cargo routes, beginning in June 2024, flying from Ürümchi’s Tianshan 3 “Tianshan” is translated as “Tengri Tagh” in Uyghur. See Mustafa Aksu, Dr. Elise Anderson, and Dr. Henryk Szadziewski. “Decolonizing the Discussion of Uyghurs: Recommendations for Journalists and Researchers,” Uyghur Human Rights Project , December 2022, online . International Airport into Bucharest (Romania), Budapest (Hungary), London, Bournemouth, and Cardiff (UK). During the same period, indirect routes emerged from Ürümchi to cities including Athens (Greece), Debrecen (Hungary), Leipzig (Germany), Liège (Belgium), Vienna (Austria), Tallinn (Estonia), and Zurich (Switzerland). The indirect routes make a short stopover in cities including Tashkent (Uzbekistan), Istanbul (Turkey), Tbilisi (Georgia), Astana, and Karaganda (Kazakhstan). Airlines that operated cargo routes between June 2024 and May 2025 between Ürümchi and Europe include Camex Airlines (Georgia), European Cargo (UK), Geo-Sky 4 Geo-Sky operated flights between July 2024 and April 2025. In a written response to a request for comment ahead of publication, Geo-Sky noted that “[D]ue to commercial considerations, we ceased operating flights to Ürümchi in April 2025 and have no plans to start operating flights to Ürümchi in the near future.” (Georgia), MNG Airlines (Turkey), My Freighter (Uzbekistan), ROMCargo (Romania), SF Airlines (China), Titan Airways (UK), and Uzbekistan Airways (Uzbekistan). 5 Flight tracking data also shows sporadic flights in this period operated by AlphaSky (1), MyWay Airlines (2), and SilkWay Airlines (3). Dozens of European routes have been launched since June 2024, meaning there are, as of May 2025, upwards of 40 flights carrying goods from the Uyghur Region to Europe weekly. 6 Flight tracking data shows additional cargo flights from Ürümchi to Belgrade, Serbia with Camex Airlines and YTO Cargo Airlines in 2025. In addition to the more regular destinations noted above, flight tracking data shows several other indirect, sporadic cargo flights from Ürümchi to Madrid and Zaragoza (Spain), Dublin (Ireland), Örebro (Sweden), Prague (Czechia), and Birmingham (UK). 7 Chinese state media report on a route from Ürümchi to Katowice, Poland (see Xinhua, “New Air‐Cargo Route Links China’s Xinjiang, Poland’s Katowice,” September 13, 2024, online ), but researchers were unable to locate these flights using flight tracking applications. Flight data even shows cargo flights originating in Ürümchi landing in New York City and Toronto after stops in Istanbul and Liège in early 2025. 8 Flight data shows that these flights are operated by MNG Airlines. In July 2025, Xinjiang Airport Group announced that new cargo flight routes from Ürümchi to Madrid and Paris are scheduled to launch in late 2025, as part of a broader expansion aimed at reaching 40 international cargo routes by the end of the year. 9 Xinhua, “Urumqi airport in China’s Xinjiang expands as key Eurasian cargo gateway,” July 21, 2025, online . Information from flight tracking websites show that each flight, from the carriers examined, can carry a maximum load of anywhere between 24 and 112 tonnes of cargo. 10 Maximum cargo capacities vary from carrier to carrier on their routes between Ürümchi and European destinations. Camex Airlines (Boeing 737, 24 tonnes); Geo-Sky (Boeing 757, 27 tonnes); My Freighter, SF Airlines, Uzbekistan Airways (Boeing 767, 52 tonnes); Titan Airways and MNG Airlines (Airbus A330 variants, 65 tonnes), European Cargo (Airbus A340, 76 tonnes); ROMCargo (Boeing 747, 112 tonnes). Source: FlightRadar24.com . In May 2025, this amounted to up to 2,000 tonnes of goods entering the EU, UK, and Switzerland from Ürümchi. Cargo flights originating in Ürümchi arriving in Europe from May 21 to May 31, 2025. The data shows a clear trend of increasing connectivity between the Uyghur Region and European markets, driven by the expansion of cargo flight routes. 11 From June 2022 to May 2024, flight tracking data shows only a few isolated cargo flights from the Uyghur Region to Europe. Researchers were only able to retrieve comprehensive historical data for the previous three years, from June 2022 to May 2025, and relied on state media and other online sources to find additional routes prior to this period. Aside from a small number of one-off flights, only two previous cargo routes, originating in Ürümchi, could be identified prior to June 2024; one in 2018 to Liège and one in 2019 to Ostrava, both of which appear discontinued. 12 ASL Airlines operated cargo flights between Ürümchi and Liège in 2018 (see Charles Kauffman, “ASL Airlines Launches First Freighter Flight to Europe from Urumqi,” Cargo Facts , August 24, 2018, online .) and EGT Express operated flights between Ürümchi and Ostrava in 2019, but based on available flight tracking data, both routes appear discontinued.
