More of this in-depth coverage Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email PARIS Almost three years after the beginning of the Gaza genocide, I am publishing a book of poetry about a house that no longer exists, in a language my mother cannot read, in a country where my family cannot follow. The first two poems I wrote in my life were called Lemon Tree and Hope. I wrote them two or three months after the genocide began in a purple notebook that my sister gave me as a gift, in my now destroyed childhood home, about a tree I will not see again. The book is named for that house, and it will be published in French on 9 September. When the collection comes out, I will be asked to sign copies of it in a city where nothing that belonged to me has ever been demolished. The book is called This is My House – in French, Ceci est ma maison. The title has a double meaning. It refers to the house in the north of Gaza where my brothers were married, where my older sisters gave birth, and where their children learned to walk on a rooftop that I could describe to you tile by tile. It also refers to Gaza, my home and the home of more than two million other people. Both have been reduced to rubble. I want to tell you how I learned that my childhood home had been destroyed because the shape of that experience is the shape of exile: It was at the end of September or early October last year when our neighbours saw the destruction. They told my family, and my family told me. That was the order. The people standing in the street knew before its owners, and I – writing a book about it – was the last to be told. Distance is not a feeling. It is a delay measurable in hours, and I have been at the far end of that delay since I crossed the border and left Gaza in July 2025. Perhaps I will be at the far end of it for the rest of my life. I was the last to find out about the destruction of my own house, where I lived since I was five. I was in my room studying when I found out, the French daylight filtering through the window in a country where the electricity does not go off, from a voice on a phone that had already said it out loud to someone else first. ◇◇◇ Nour ElAssy/TNH One of Nour's notebooks on a rooftop in the Gaza Strip. Everything that was in the house was lost. The oil paintings I had made and never showed to anyone – some of them finished, some still works in progress. My books in three languages, Arabic, English, and French. The room I wrote in. The walls that held space for weddings and births. The rooftop. The particular way the afternoon light came into the kitchen. A house is not just a structure. It is a set of instructions for where the light falls in space, and those instructions have been deleted from the world. There is no copy. Except one. It is not a good copy, but it is what remains, consisting of over 50 poems in a language I was not born into. The poems are not gentle memories. I have not been able to write about anything except this: the house; the yearning for what no longer exists; what has been done to the people who called it home; the children killed in numbers that stopped being numbers; massacres that have names in Arabic and no names at all in the papers here; a boy who is now alone in the world because everyone who knew his name was killed on the same afternoon and who is expected to keep waking up. I did not choose these subjects. There was nothing else in the room. I wrote the poems for myself and for my family. That was the readership I imagined. I did not intend to create a manuscript. The poems were phrases in notebooks I already owned and that I was already using for something else. There are French verb tables in those notebooks and lecture notes. I was not making a book. I was catching sentences before they disappeared like everything else. When I started writing the poems I was a student of English and French literature. My university’s campus was destroyed, like virtually all the university campuses in Gaza. The university continued teaching online throughout the genocide, and I continued attending – which sounds absurd. So was scrawling half a line of a poem about a dead child at the top of a page about the subjunctive. I was not making a book. I was catching sentences before they disappeared like everything else. I wrote the poems in English even though Arabic is my first language. I’ve never been able to fully account for that. Maybe writing in a foreign language allows for more emotional distance. The words land with less force. The pictures they summon are dimmer. English was not a literary choice. It was a pane of glass. In Arabic, everything would have been too close and loud. Dimmer is what I needed. English was not a literary choice. It was a pane of glass. In Arabic, everything would have been too close and loud. In English, I could stand on the other side and look in. Every poem in this book was written through that pane of glass by a woman who could not have written a word of it without that separation. But that pane of glass also disappears, even in a second language, when I write about my mother or my younger sister. I can write in English about a child I never met, but I cannot say my own address out loud. ◇◇◇ The poems left me before any publisher was interested. I started reciting them on Instagram while I was still in Gaza. People responded, and I liked that they responded. Some of the notebooks I wrote the poems in were destroyed with the house. Some stayed behind with my sister. What is being published is what escaped from a fire and across the borders. My first book is the surviving portion of something that was never assembled. There is a moment in every one of these conversations where the interviewer asks a perfectly reasonable question and I cannot answer. Then it was translated, and the translation is extraordinary. Lisa Ducasse did what I would have told you could not be done. Writers I know and trust, Karim Kattan among them, have said so too, and they are right. I want to state my admiration without a single qualifier attached to it. And still, reading it, I meet a stranger who knows everything about me. Now, I sit down for interviews to talk about the book. There is a moment in every one of these conversations where the interviewer asks a perfectly reasonable question and I cannot answer. I stop. The kind person across from me waits. The waiting becomes its own weather in the room because now I have made them uncomfortable, and I find myself apologising to someone for the destruction of my own street. At the launch event in Paris, there will be a table with volumes of the book piled high. My name will be said into a microphone. People will be genuinely moved, and then they will go home, which is the correct thing for them to do and I hold it against nobody. There will be a picture of me smiling, and the smile will be real because this is the thing every writer is supposed to want, and there was a girl in that house who wanted it more than she wanted almost anything else. At the same time, my mother will not be in the room, nor will my younger sister. Neither can read the language the book is printed in. Both of these things are true at once, and neither cancels out the other: This is my dream, and it has been handed to me in exchange for everything I had. Nobody consulted me on the rate. ◇◇◇ There is one more thing – the worst of all – which I am going to set down ra

https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/inves.body: Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email PARIS and KHAN YOUNIS, occupied Palestinian territories At home in southeastern Gaza, Ammouna Ahmad Abu Irjila used to begin her days at dawn, checking on her fields after the morning prayer. Before her family was forcibly displaced, Abu Irjila farmed four dunams – about 4,000 square metres, or one acre – inherited from her father in Khuza’a, a small agricultural town near the border with Israel. At a glance: Israel’s demolition of eastern Gaza A months-long analysis of satellite imagery points to Israel creating a blank slate where Palestinian communities once stood and then establishing infrastructure to maintain a long-term presence in the areas of eastern Gaza it controls. Entire towns have been ground into dust, and Israel has recently begun setting fire to kilometres-wide areas of cropland in the 65% of Gaza under its direct control. Israel is building infrastructure – including military bases and roads – on the cleared land where houses, schools, hospitals, cemeteries, and farms once stood. This could align with two competing visions for eastern Gaza: preparation for redevelopment through the US-backed Board of Peace, or a wasteland under indefinite Israeli control. Given the rhetoric from senior Israeli politicians, the lack of progress on the US ceasefire roadmap, and insight from aid workers familiar with conversations about reconstruction, the second scenario is more likely. In both scenarios, the property rights of Palestinians who owned homes and land in the demolished communities are being entirely neglected. The demolition has involved numerous violations of international law, and is evidence of war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide, according to legal experts. “I didn’t even know what it meant to sleep after sunrise,” said Abu Irjila, 73. She grew up in Khuza’a and raised six children there. Some also became farmers, renting land nearby and selling their produce in local markets. The homes and landscape where all of this life took place have now been entirely wiped out. Since the October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas, Israeli forces have stepped up a systematic campaign of erasure in the area of Gaza directly under their control, which they have expanded from 54% when the deal was signed to now about 65%. In this almost entirely depopulated zone, Israel has been tearing down whatever remains, setting fire to fields, and bulldozing towns and once-green agricultural communities into the ground. The New Humanitarian has spent more than six months monitoring and analysing satellite imagery to document Israel’s clearing of land and subsequent construction activities, focusing on some of the most-affected areas in eastern Gaza, and speaking to Palestinians who lived in the communities being erased. The pattern of activity suggests Israel is creating a blank slate and establishing infrastructure to maintain a long-term presence in the areas of eastern Gaza it controls – what senior aid workers say could be the groundwork for annexation. Rhetoric from Israel’s political leadership points in that direction as well. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the military to expand its control of Gaza to 70% of the Strip, and his defence minister has said Israeli troops will remain indefinitely. Other government ministers are pushing to re-establish Israeli settlements there. In the process, the property rights of Palestinians who lived on and owned the land, like Abu Irjila, are being neglected and usurped. Such extensive demolition is abnormal in modern warfare – especially during what is supposed to be a cessation of hostilities – according to Adil Haque, an expert in international law at Rutgers University in the US. “I can’t think of another example of it,” said Haque. Satellite imagery via Planet Labs PBC Destroying civilian homes in this way is illegal under international law, which allows property destruction only where the military can show it was necessary, and then only to an extent proportional to the military advantage gained – which is plainly not the case here, Haque added. The destruction implicates Israel in multiple potential war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to several legal experts The New Humanitarian consulted. It is also evidence for the legal argument that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, according to Muna Haddad, a lawyer with Adalah, a Palestinian-run legal rights centre based in Israel. “It is part of the genocide, part of deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about physical destruction,” Haddad said, echoing language from the definition of genocide in the UN convention codifying the crime. Neither the Israeli military nor the Israeli government responded to The New Humanitarian’s request for comment on the legality of these demolitions, Israel’s plans for the future of Gaza, or on other details of this investigation. The Israeli military has previously said extensive demolitions in Gaza are necessary for Israel’s security “to prevent the enemy from carrying out offensive terrorist activities, such as those seen in the October 7 massacre, or launching fire towards Israeli settlements”. It has claimed it does not target civilian infrastructure and that “all actions are carried out in compliance with international law”. Brad Klapper, a spokesperson for the Board of Peace, the US-backed entity authorised by the UN to oversee the administration of Gaza during the ceasefire, told The New Humanitarian in a statement that the Board is “deeply concerned by continued reports of destruction of civilian property, damage to agricultural land, and the displacement of Palestinian families in Gaza”, and that “the protection of civilians, civilian infrastructure, and property rights is central to any credible stabilisation and reconstruction effort”. Aid workers familiar with conversations about reconstruction, however, describe deeply frustrating efforts to convince US officials to consider the rights of people in Gaza. At the same time, they say the US-led redevelopment plans on the table are not remotely viable, and are being torpedoed by Israeli officials who they believe would prefer to see Gaza in ruins, with rebuilding only where it suits their interests. The Palestinians whose property and land is being demolished say they are being entirely left out of these conversations. “You can’t take my land and do what you want without asking me, without giving me any kind of [compensation], or giving me another place or another piece of land. It’s forbidden under international law, and even [Palestinian] local law,” said Samir Zaqout, the Gaza-based deputy director of the Al Mezan Center for Human Rights. “No one cares about this. And I don’t know what they are thinking – because no one will tolerate this when it comes to the land in future. Even the people themselves, they will try to do something to defend their rights, to defend themselves. And it means that you open this place up to be in a circle of violence forever,” Zaqout said. Ghada Abdulfattah/TNH Ghada Abdulfattah/TNH Left: Ammouna Ahmad Abu Irjila by a patch of land where she has planted a garden near the displacement tent where she now lives. Right: Abu Irjila showing a photo on her phone of her working her farm in Khuza'a, which has now been entirely destroyed. The reconstruction mirage Two years of Israeli bombardment up until October 2025 had already created unprecedented destruction throughout Gaza. Behind the front line, troops and contractors armed with explosives and US-made Caterpillar bulldozers had been working relentlessly to erase the physical traces of Palestinian life, obliterating towns from Rafah in the south to Beit Hanoun in the north. https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/featu.body: Home Asia Iran Related stories Conflict Opinion 11 September 2026 Visible crises, invisible people Conflict Analysis 9 September 2026 Finding a path to peace: Nigeria’s long, faltering history of dialogue with Boko Haram Conflict News 7 September 2026 EXCLUSIVE: Nigerian government and Boko Haram strike secret ceasefire deal Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email TEHRAN × 1,000 tomans is 10,000 rials, and many people use this unofficial currency unit because inflation in Iran is so high. The past six months of bombs, geopolitical tensions and the looming threat of a wider conflict have created a suffocating sense of uncertainty for many Iranians. And it’s not just about the airstrikes. Young people say the period since the US and Israel first struck their country in late February has been one of anxiety-inducing limbo, with their futures put on hold indefinitely. The New Humanitarian spoke to five young Iranians in the capital, who shared what it feels like to be trapped, watching their best years slip away. From cancelled weddings and crushing unemployment to never-ending news updates and the vanishing of simple pleasures, their stories offer a window into what it is like to live through a war that has taken away their ability to plan for tomorrow. In Tehran and across the country, fresh US and Iranian strikes this week were a stark reminder that, after half a year of bombing and a war of words between the US and Iran, ceasefire talks remain stalled. The Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut, while the core issues driving the conflict remain unresolved. Iranian citizens have been left bracing for hostilities to resume at any moment. In the 40 days after the US and Israel launched attacks in late February, more than 3,500 people – including hundreds of civilians – were killed, according to the Iranian government. While Iran’s economy has struggled for years amid sanctions , US economic pressure and the war have compounded the pain. Iranian officials have put the economic damage from the war at more than $270 billion , though the figure is a preliminary estimate. Inflation reached nearly 88% year-over-year in July with the rial hitting a record low on 2 September , while sweeping corporate budget cuts have triggered mass layoffs; more than a million people in a country of 87 million are believed to have lost their jobs . Even when the skies over Tehran are quiet, the five young people whose words are featured here – Ziba, Nima, Fatema, Sima, and Amir Ali* – say the agony has shifted beyond the bombing itself. What weighs most heavily now is the paralysis of not knowing what comes next. Names have been changed due to security concerns, and words have been translated, condensed, and edited for clarity. Ziba, 27, watched her wedding plans fell apart “Every major milestone in my life has been frozen” My morning routine now begins before my feet even touch the floor. The very first thing I do when I wake up is grab my phone and open my main news channels. I have to scroll through everything posted overnight. The news cycle here changes by the minute. You might go to bed reading that a diplomatic agreement is imminent, only to wake up and find out that infrastructure was bombed while you were sleeping. I have to know exactly what reality I am waking up into. The initial shock we felt when this first started has morphed into something else, but there are still moments that completely rattle me. It’s terrifying when I go outside and see massive lines of people panic-buying fuel at the petrol stations. I look at them and think, “What will happen to the city if they strike tomorrow?” My nights are consumed by a different kind of anxiety. A few months ago, I didn't even know what [the live online flight tracker] Flightradar was. Now, before I can attempt to sleep, I am on the app monitoring the airspace over the Middle East. I check to see if civilian planes are still flying over Iran, or if flights are still landing in Israel. If I see commercial planes in the sky, I tell myself it's safe enough to close my eyes. Even our family group chats offer no escape; they are a constant stream of terrifying rumours. Someone will forward a fake message claiming a nuclear strike is coming tonight, alongside advice to hoard food or buy power generators. To cope with the overwhelming dread, I downloaded half a dozen mindless puzzle games on my phone. But the stress gave me such severe insomnia that I used to wake up multiple times a night just to check the news. Now, I have to take sleeping pills. When the anxiety becomes too heavy, I put on a podcast and play the puzzle games for hours, waiting for the medication to finally make my eyes heavy enough to sleep. Every major milestone in my life has been frozen. My fiancé and I got engaged exactly 40 days before this recent wave of conflict began. We were deep into planning the wedding, but it completely fell apart. How can you book a venue, buy a wedding dress, or put down deposits when you don’t know if a war will break out tomorrow? We have stopped all planning and will probably just move into our apartment quietly without a celebration. It breaks my heart because I had to let what was supposed to be one of the best nights of my life go. Even my smallest daily joys have vanished. I used to be obsessed with online shopping and skincare routines. I haven't bought anything in months. I am literally scraping the last drops out of my old makeup containers. Every time I think about restocking, I stop myself. I need to hoard every rial in case the economy collapses and I get laid off. And honestly, what is the point of a skincare routine if a war breaks out? When I hang out with my friends, the panic has been replaced by a heavy numbness. Six months ago, we took every threat seriously. Now, if someone reads a headline out loud about an impending attack or a peace talk, we just laugh. We have become completely desensitised. Underneath that numbness is a profound grief. The prime years of our youth — the years we should be growing and experiencing life — are being destroyed by the egos of global powers who do not care about regular people. Nima, 21, fears his attempt to leave Iran has set him back “The sheer terror of being completely left behind” For the past two years, my life has been defined by a single, obsessive goal: to emigrate from Iran by the time I turn 21. I took a massive risk and dropped out of university to make this happen. I work in video production and editing now, and every decision I’ve made since leaving school – every late night staring at editing deadlines, every rial I’ve desperately managed to save, every expensive language class I’ve paid for – has been dedicated to preparing for a visa interview at the French embassy and securing a way out. But since the conflict escalated last year, and with this endless, agonising cycle of ceasefires and new threats, my carefully constructed roadmap has been thrown into absolute chaos. The uncertainty we are living through isn't just an abstract political talking point on the news; it is a solid brick wall standing between me and my future. I am supposed to be finalising my paperwork right now, but I wake up every morning paralysed by questions I cannot answer. If I am finally ready for my visa interview next month, will the foreign embassies in Tehran even be open? Are they quietly evacuating their diplomatic staff right now? Will any country even issue visas to young Iranians right now, or are we considered too high-risk? You just don’t know, and that not-knowing is suffocating. Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email Editor’s note: This is the first in a series of reports exploring the feasibility of dialogue as a path to peace in Africa’s protracted civil conflicts. MAIDUGURI, Nigeria A ceasefire agreement with the jihadist group Boko Haram has been in effect for the past three months and is expected to be extended, but has not been previously reported publicly, The New Humanitarian has learned. The agreement is linked to hostage negotiations that secured the release in June of 360 civilians abducted by the group from Ngoshe village, in the foothills of the Mandara mountains on the border with Cameroon. The mass kidnapping occurred in March during a Boko Haram attack on a nearby army base. Three people with contacts among Boko Haram members, some of them senior figures, independently told The New Humanitarian that a truce had been in effect since June and was likely to be extended for a further 40 days. Communities in the Ngoshe area – regular victims of Boko Haram predation – say attacks have stopped since the ceasefire, according to two of the sources. The deal that freed the villagers also reportedly included a ransom payment of five billion naira ($3.7 million) by the government, a transaction Abuja has denied amid controversy over the alleged misappropriation of some of the money. The New Humanitarian reached out to spokespeople for the government, defence headquarters, and the army to verify reports of a ceasefire, but received no reply prior to publishing. What remains unclear is the longer-term significance of any agreement. “It could be just a temporary, tactical ceasefire that benefits both sides, but doesn’t really affect the trajectory of the war,” said conflict researcher Malik Samuel. “I don’t think it’s a step towards a sustainable peace settlement.” The deal does not involve so-called Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), an offshoot and rival to Boko Haram, based on the islands of Lake Chad and a rural swathe of northeastern Borno State. Clashes have continued between the two groups. After 17 years of a war that has indirectly cost close to 350,000 civilian lives, the idea of negotiations with Boko Haram – officially Jama’at Ahl al Sunna li Da’wa wal Jihad (JAS) – and other armed groups sharply divides Nigerians. Those living closest to the conflict tend to be far more supportive of dialogue than the rest of the country. However, the government’s public position is an emphatic rejection of talks with a group legally proscribed as a terrorist organisation. President Bola Tinubu has instead announced the beefing up of an overstretched army – an initiative related to elections early next year in which public safety will be a key issue. The promised 30,000 new recruits and four extra divisions will provide the “teeth that are needed to defeat terrorism and banditry”, Tinubu said in July. Nevertheless, behind the scenes, “the government seems very interested in having a dialogue with Boko Haram, perhaps realising a military response alone is inadequate to resolving the problem,” noted Samuel. When rebels rule: ISWAP’s formula for winning support in Nigeria’s northeast The jihadist group poses more than a military challenge to the Nigerian government – its hearts and minds campaign is also a political threat. “Both sides believe a settlement is possible” Since the Boko Haram insurgency began in 2009, there has been a long if faltering history of under the radar dialogue approaches, according to security officials, diplomats, and mediators, who spoke to The New Humanitarian on the condition of anonymity so they could talk freely. “Both sides believe a settlement is possible,” a diplomat with knowledge of the chronology of contacts told The New Humanitarian. “For all parties, a non-kinetic [military] approach is intellectually acceptable. But they still believe that by improving their military situations they can influence those negotiations.” Those talks have been led on the government’s side by the Office of the National Security Advisor and the spy agency, the Department of State Services. They have repeatedly failed, typically scuppered by spoilers within the government and military, forcing the parties to rebuild confidence each time. Historically, “we’ve negotiated a couple of ceasefires but they couldn’t be maintained,” said a government security official with knowledge of the dialogue process. “The last hudna [armistice] was in the 2022/2023 period but it also collapsed.” The current agreement may suffer the same fate. Two sources who told The New Humanitarian about the deal warned that Boko Haram may be using the ceasefire to strengthen its position, potentially by moving “equipment” into the Mandera mountains. Can dialogue with jihadist groups bring peace to the Sahel? Warfighting has only deepened wounds, hardened divides, and fuelled new insurgencies – a rethink is long overdue. Who’s who Boko Haram is headed by Ibrahim Bakura Doro , the overall commander and imam (religious leader), based on the islands on the northern section of Lake Chad, on the Niger Republic border. Boko Haram has three factions , all of which have sworn allegiance to Bakura: Darul Gazwa, operating in southeastern Borno and headed by Alhai Kale; the Sadiku group of Abubakar Sadiku Saidu, active around north-central Nigeria; and the Ali Ngulde faction, which carried out the Ngoshe kidnappings. The success of the ceasefire depends on whether Bakura, from his Lake Chad base thousands of kilometres away, can yoke the three other Boko Haram commanders into a sustainable deal. Rival ISWAP is operationally and organisationally distinct from Boko Haram, its jihadist cousin. While Boko Haram survives on looting and extorting civilians – a practice known as fey'u – plundering is banned by ISWAP. Boko Haram is also more locally focused whereas ISWAP – among the most active of so-called Islamic State-Central’s franchises – is loyal to the transnational “caliphate”, which effectively hands IS-Central veto power over any dialogue initiative, according to people familiar with the group. “ISWAP needs buy-in from IS. They make the final decision,” a rehabilitated former ISWAP commander told The New Humanitarian. “But Bakura needs money, you can make a deal with him.” Splits and rivalries: A timeline of Boko Haram/ISWAP discord Boko Haram began as an ultra-conservative religious movement in the early 2000s in Maiduguri under a young cleric, Mohammed Yusuf. It tapped into a radical zeitgeist that appealed across classes – condemning so-called “Western values” and celebrating 500 years of Islamic learning and empire in Nigeria’s northeast. Initially, Yusuf resisted calling for jihad, but as tensions with the authorities increased, he launched an urban insurrection in July 2009. It was quickly crushed, and Yusuf was extrajudicially killed by the police. Abubakar Shekau, his deputy, took over as imam. A wave of bombings, kidnappings, and the overrunning of towns had the army on the backfoot, and rural Borno emptied as people were displaced from their homes. Shekau declared allegiance to so-called Islamic State in 2015 and the group was renamed Islamic State of West Africa Province (ISWAP). In 2016, ISWAP split. Dissident commanders led by Abu Musa al-Barnawi and cleric Mamman Nur accused Shekau of despotism and condemned his use of “takfir” – the death penalty for infidels – against rural civilians. Bitter factional fighting followed, but the dissidents managed to establish themselves in the Lake Chad region and win the blessing of IS-Central. Shekau reverted to his group’s previous Boko Haram designation. Better resourced and discip

https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/featu.body: Home Asia Pakistan This article is also available in Arabic Share & more Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email LAHORE In their two-room tin-roof house in one of the many shanty towns that dot Lahore, in eastern Pakistan , Ilyas and Nasim Masih and their seven daughters, aged three to 15, eke out an existence dependent on Ilyas’s meagre income as a day labourer. The youngest children play at the feet of their parents, running a small piece of brightly painted wood up and down the floor, pretending it is a car. The children have few other toys and share between them a crude rag doll made by their aunt and a few other odds and ends. “I have never ridden in a car or any vehicle, but I see them go by on the roads and would love to sit in one,” Selina, aged six, told IRIN. The chances of that happening are small. Ilyas earns on average Rs 3,000 (US$36) a month. “Sometimes people want trenches dug or help to move furniture, and they pay me small amounts to do this. Some days I sit idle. I struggle even to buy a single kilo of `atta’ [wheat flour], which costs Rs 30 [36 US cents], and even that produces just about half a `roti’ [flat bread] for each of us,” he said. For Ilyas’s family, securing each meal - eaten on the floor around a kerosene oil stove on which Nasim cooks - is an ordeal. “Especially at night, it is painful to hear the children beg for more food . Sometimes they snatch food from each other,” Ilyas said. Nasim said her neighbours had suggested they sell a child but “I shudder to think what fate my daughter would meet if we resort to this.” She said if they had a son it would be different because they could send him out to work, “but with only girls, we simply don’t know what to do.” The eldest two girls help out in the home and fetch water from a nearby tap, as there is no running water or power in their home. “It is unthinkable I could sell our children, but sometimes I wonder what on earth we are to do,” Ilyas said. Though Ilyas and Nasim said they would never contemplate selling a child, they know how desperation can dictate actions. “Our cousin who lives just outside Lahore sold a kidney to try and make ends meet,” Ilyas said. “He was sick afterwards and could not work, so he sold his 14-year-old daughter for Rs 50,000 [$600] to a man who said he wanted to marry her. The man was over 50, and after a month he sent the girl out to work as a prostitute. Essentially, this is that man’s business. My cousin knew, but he had no choice.” Photo: Kamila Hyat/IRIN Ilyas Masih with one of his seven daughters; feeding so many is not easy Poverty driving child sales In other cases middlemen go to impoverished families and buy children for slave labour or sex work, said Ilyas. There are reports that rising poverty is forcing a growing number of families to sell children, with girls in particular ending up in sex work. “We have more and more reports of people selling their children due to poverty,” I.A. Rehman, secretary-general of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP), told IRIN. Boys were sometimes trafficked outside the country, and girls were generally sold into the sex trade, he said. According to HRCP, growing unemployment is a big factor contributing to poverty. According to independent estimates , the unemployment rate is 15.2 percent. Poverty levels have remained persistently high in Pakistan. According to a study completed in February 2010 by economists at the Lahore University of Management Sciences, every second household in the districts of the southern Punjab, comprising 17.49 million people, lives in absolute poverty. The fact that many wage earners have lower skill levels, due to a lack of education, is cited as a key factor in this. “For households in the north [of Punjab Province], 14.26 percent of their income comes from remittances, which explains their comparative affluence; it is 4.4 percent in the centre [of the province], 2.14 percent in the south and 3.03 percent in the west,” the study says. Punjab is by far the most populous of Pakistan’s four provinces. “Pakistan’s economy has been in recession for some years. Because of political instability and terrorism there is no investment and no growth. This means fewer jobs and other related issues,” economic analyst Sikander Lodhi told IRIN. He also said prices of many items, including food, had risen in response to rising fuel costs. Social taboos But this does not stop an average poor family from having many children. Nasim said “social taboos” prevented them from using contraception and keeping their family size smaller so there would be fewer mouths to feed. “It is common for families not to use contraception. Men say going on the pill may make women promiscuous by encouraging them to have sex outside marriage, and they decline to use condoms themselves,” Javeria Ali, a gynaecologist who works at a community clinic in Lahore, told IRIN. “Married men who buy condoms are sniggered at. Besides, I can’t afford it,” said Ilyas, who is a Christian. “Children are given by God. We should not stop this. It is wrong to do so.” None of their daughters goes to school, as Ilyas said he could not afford books, uniforms or stationery. The parents of girls are by tradition expected to host feasts and when they get married provide a dowry that usually includes electronic gadgets and household items. “I have no idea what their future will be as I cannot fund their marriages. Even we who are so poor generally spend at least Rs 100,000 ($1,200) on a wedding. We must borrow from neighbours and relatives, and then somehow pay back the debt,” said Ilyas. Sex work For brothel owner Farzana Baig (not her real name), her two-storey house in a posh area of Lahore is the end of the road for desperate families wishing to sell their daughters into sex work. She said a number of girls were “sold by parents in rural areas, especially in the southern Punjab”. Often the girls were told they were being sent to the city to work or attend classes. “These people are so poor, they have no choice. To feed their other children, they must sell one or maybe more,” Baig said, adding that some of the girls “are so thin when they arrive I have to feed them for a week so they look healthier and more attractive”. Though prostitution and child labour in the sex industry are both against the law, Baig houses five to six under-age girls and several older sex workers. “There is a big demand for young girls; we take in those as young as 10. Customers pay well for pre-pubescent children,” she said. “The local cops pose no problems. I pay them off each month.” Sheena Bibi, 36 and widowed when she was only 20, told IRIN that sex work had almost become a tradition in her family due to extreme poverty. “My father was a drug addict and my mother prostituted herself to put food on the table. I did the same for years and today my two teenage daughters work the streets. Now they support us all,” she said. Bibi said she tried to avoid sending her girls out into the streets but to meet the rising cost of food “no other work pays quite as well, and I am too old now to do it myself”. The girls, aged 13 and 15, approach established customers working in various markets in Lahore, and are paid around Rs 50 [60 US cents] for each encounter, usually carried out in small rooms behind shops. “They don’t like being fondled or touched or having sex, but they are now used to it,” said Bibi. There is scant data on the number of child sex workers in Pakistan. The subject has long been taboo. A 2001 report by the government’s National Commission for Child Welfare and Development was the first official admission that child sex workers exist. Anecdotal evidence, however, suggests it is widespread. “During the day I work as a maid, but at night I `serve’ clients. It helps my family, and I can send home more money to them,” said Asiya Bibi, 14, whose parents and four younger siblings are based in

https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/inves.body: Home Middle East and North Africa Palestine Related stories Conflict Feature 27 August 2026 Nine years on, a Rohingya survivor revisits the massacre that killed her family, and dreams of going home Human Rights Opinion 25 August 2026 Landmark ICC trial on Libya migrant abuses must lead to more scrutiny of EU complicity Human Rights Feature 24 August 2026 What one group of Afghan women and their supporters make of international engagement with the Taliban Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email LONDON Google and Meta have run over 100,000 advertisements for businesses that the UN says are facilitating illegal Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank. The New Humanitarian cross-referenced both tech-giants’ ad libraries with a UN human rights office database listing 158 firms involved in construction, demolition, surveillance, resource extraction, and pollution in the occupied Palestinian territory. Of these, 39 firms purchased ad space from Google and Meta after they were added to the UN list. Another three firms bought ads before they were listed. At least seven of these businesses recently promoted products and services directly related to settlement, including housing, an expedited gun license programme, and machinery used in the demolition of Palestinian property. Other firms’ ads are less explicitly tied to settlement. Israel’s national water company, Mekorot, has advertised infrastructure projects that span both Israel and occupied areas. The accommodation platforms Booking.com, Airbnb, and Tripadvisor – all listed by the UN for “supporting the maintenance and existence of settlements” – account for most of the ads. Israel’s West Bank settlements, including in East Jerusalem, are widely considered illegal under international law. Expert legal opinion views the settlements as a violation of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which prohibits the transfer of civilians into the occupied territory, and thus views these actions as a war crime. In July 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territories is illegal and must be brought to an end “as rapidly as possible”. This is not the first time tech giants have been accused of running digital ads related to Israeli activities in occupied Palestine. A 2025 investigation by Al Jazeera exposed Meta ads promoting settlement housing and seeking donations for Israeli military units active in the Gaza Strip. But previous coverage of these digital ads has either focused on specific tech platforms or specific companies buying ad space. This investigation has identified dozens of such companies and represents the most systematic examination of the digital advertising ecosystem aiding Israel’s occupation of the West Bank to date. It sheds light on a crucial yet undercovered digital and financial aspect of Israel’s colonisation of the West Bank. Alongside its destruction and occupation of the Gaza Strip in response to attacks by the militant group Hamas in late 2023, Israel has also presided over record-high settlement expansion , skyrocketing violence by Israeli settlers, and moves towards “ de facto annexation ” in the West Bank. “Corporations operating in armed conflict zones bear a heightened duty of due diligence to avoid contributing to or profiting from violations of international law,” said Shahd Hammouri, an international law lecturer at the University of Kent. Providing a platform for organisations flagged by the UN for their activities in illegal settlements, Hammouri added, “constitutes a clear failure of their due diligence obligations”. The ads may violate the tech giants’ own guidelines. Meta’s ad rules “forbid organisations or individuals that proclaim a violent mission or are engaged in violence to have a presence on our platforms”. Google’s policy forbids ads that incite “hatred against, promotes discrimination of, or disparages an individual or group on the basis of their race or ethnic origin, religion, disability... or any other characteristic that is associated with systemic discrimination or marginalization”. Rasha Abdul-Rahim, a technology and human rights expert, said the platforms’ tolerance of pro-settlement ads, plus their censorship of evidence of alleged Israeli crimes, amounts to a “systematic effort” to promote Israeli policy goals at the expense of their own rules. Representatives at Meta and Google, including the latter’s ad liaison, Ginny Marvin, did not respond to questions about their review processes for West Bank settlement ads or their potential complicity in violations of international law. Expedited gun licenses Google is hosting a Hebrew-language ad campaign for Caliber 3, a company based in the Gush Etzion settlement bloc, south of Jerusalem, which has been described by Israel’s Haaretz newspaper as an “ anti-terror fantasy camp ”. Caliber 3 is listed in the UN database for providing security services and equipment to illegal settlements. Its offerings also include a gun shop and a shooting range for tourists. Its Google ads, some of which were still active in April 2026, promote an “expedited gun license” programme at the shooting range, offering “full support throughout the process” of obtaining a private firearms qualification. Only Israeli citizens are eligible for the qualification , despite Caliber 3’s presence on Palestinian territory. The licensing criteria measure an applicant’s suitability based on residency and work in “eligible locations” that are exposed to potential risks, effectively categorising West Bank settlers as the most in need of firearms. The Google ads guide users to Caliber 3’s website , where they can book the accelerated licensing programme or view a range of “tourist experiences”. Caliber 3’s “ IDF Shooting Adventure ” is marketed as an educational experience, allowing patrons “to learn about the most moral army in the world”. Caliber 3 describes the experience as “perfect for family and friends” and “suitable for visitors aged 4+”. The website shows glowing reviews of their tourist programmes, primarily from American visitors. Participants are able to use .22 calibre rifles and 12-gauge shotguns to shoot at cutouts of “terrorists”. Videos on Caliber 3’s website show that these targets depict Arab men wearing the keffiyeh, a Palestinian scarf. “IDF Shooting Adventure” on Caliber 3’s website The firm has close ties to Israel’s military and political establishment. Owner and founder Sharon Gat is described on the company’s website as a colonel in a special forces unit of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). He regularly appears in Israeli and international media campaigning for the expansion of firearms licensing and the use of aggressive “counter-terror” operations in the West Bank. Most other employees are either former or active IDF service members, and two have held senior security positions within the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office. Caliber 3’s ad campaign on Google coincides with a sharp rise in settler attacks against Palestinians, including shootings and physical assaults. The attacks have followed a state-backed effort to arm settlers across the West Bank. Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister, has publicly celebrated the approval of more than 240,000 new gun permits since he pushed to expand licensing in 2023, compared with around 8,000 annually in previous years. “The overwhelming majority of settlers we are now facing are holding some kind of weapon,” Manal Tamimi, a human rights activist and resident of the Palestinian village of Nabi Saleh, told The New Humanitarian. “We didn’t see this before.” Amid escalating settler violence against Palestinians and impunity for the perpetrators , private firearms qualifications are “not a license for a weapon, but a license to kill Palestinians”, Tamimi said. https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-.body: Home Africa DRC Related stories Aid and Policy Investigations 29 September 2020 EXCLUSIVE: More than 50 women accuse aid workers of sex abuse in Congo Ebola crisis Aid and Policy Investigations 18 June 2020 How ‘Ebola business’ threatens aid operations in Congo Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email BUNIA & GOMA, Democratic Republic of the Congo A large-scale response has begun to an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo that went undetected for up to two months and has already become one of the largest on record, with 671 suspected cases and 160 suspected deaths. But funding limitations for the Congolese government and international responders, political and security dynamics in the outbreak zone, and troubled responses to past Ebola epidemics in DRC are raising concerns about efforts to contain the spread. “We are trying to fight the disease with the equipment and resources available in order to save our people, who have already suffered from insecurity for a long time and now face a new ordeal,” said Chérubin Radjabu, a nurse in the outbreak area. The epidemic, centred in Ituri province but with cases in North Kivu, South Kivu, and neighbouring Uganda, involves the extremely rare Bundibugyo variant, for which there have been only two past outbreaks and are no approved vaccines or treatments. The severity of the situation led World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus to fast-track the declaration on 17 May of a public health emergency of international concern, which allows for greater mobilisation of resources. A zoonotic disease that spreads from animals to humans, and then between people, Ebola is less transmissible than many other infectious diseases, spreading through direct contact with an infected person’s blood or body fluids. WHO says the outbreak does not pose a pandemic threat, but still presents a severe national and regional health risk, given the up to 50% fatality rate of Bundibugyo, and the lack of vaccines and therapeutics, which are available for other strains. To deal with the threat, treatment centres are now being set up, isolation tents installed in hospitals, and medical supplies shipped to the outbreak zone, alongside responders from the Congolese health ministry and international organisations. DRC has contained 16 previous Ebola outbreaks and has world-leading expertise, but past responses have also struggled, most notably to a 2018-2020 North Kivu-centred flare up, which was the first to unfold in an active conflict zone and became the second-worst outbreak in history. The current epidemic is also unfolding in conflict-affected areas, as well as amid global aid cuts and a fraught political situation in the country, all of which could significantly complicate the response. “A race against time” Of chief concern is tracking cases and determining the true extent of the outbreak, with modelling by Imperial College London suggesting there could already be more than 1,000 infections. Though it is unclear who patient zero is, the first known case died at a medical centre in Bunia, the Ituri capital, on 24 April. He was then buried 70 kilometres away in Mongbwalu, where mourners touched the body, unaware he had died from Ebola. By the time an outbreak was declared on 15 May – following prolonged testing delays and transportation mishaps – people had been travelling around for weeks, making it difficult to figure out who had contact with those infected. “Unfortunately, this was addressed very late,” said Claire Nicolet, an emergency coordinator with Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). “It's going to be a real race against time to try and trace the contacts who may have travelled and even crossed borders.” Mongbwalu, the current epicentre, is a mining town that hosts thousands of artisanal diggers who work to extract small amounts of gold. A growing number of fatalities have been recorded there in recent days. “There have been many deaths; today, I’ve seen several funerals, all without any protective equipment,” Daniel Mupenda, a miner who works in the town, said on 17 May in a telephone interview. Issa Hassan, a Bunia resident who is secretary to the Ituri governor, said fear has taken hold over many people in his city – a commercial hub of hundreds of thousands of people – and he is wondering if his children should be attending school. “The authorities are taking this very seriously, and the minister of health came from Kinshasa to assess the response capacity,” Hassan said. “But we are going to need the help of international partners.” Other residents of Bunia have still been going about their daily activities. Churches have been full, roadside vendors are at work, and motorcycle taxis continue to carry passengers and goods. In health facilities, however, the strain is more visible. MSF has reported that isolation wards are full, leaving some patients behind in the community and increasing the risk of further transmission. Kahongya, the nurse who specialises in infection control in Bunia, said health workers are facing multiple challenges: insufficient protective equipment, a lack of funding, and transport and access constraints in some affected areas. Still, he said local health facilities have the capacity to deal with the situation “thanks to the experience gained during previous Ebola outbreaks and the COVID-19 pandemic”. Serge Kambale Sivyavugha, a researcher and general practitioner, cautioned that there is a lack of a ”sufficiently resilient health system prepared to deal with this type of epidemic” because past responses have not built enough capacity on the ground. “When interventions are managed exclusively from the central level and rely mainly on external teams, they do not strengthen the local system,” he said. “On the contrary, they create a dependency that becomes problematic as soon as these actors disperse.” Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters A Congolese police personnel stands guard at the burning Ebola treatment center in Rwampara General Hospital near Bunia, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of Congo, 21 May 2026. A limited toolkit The second major concern is how to manage the outbreak without a licensed vaccine and approved treatments — key tools that have significantly improved responses to other Ebola strains. Speaking to journalists including The New Humanitarian in Bunia on 21 May, Jean Kaseya, head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said “a major vaccine research programme” is now underway with international partners. Still, responders will be relying for now on core public health measures to break transmission, such as early case detection, isolation, contact tracing, and safe burials. These measures have controlled many previous outbreaks in DRC. Some fear global aid cuts could hamper the response, just as they may have weakened DRC’s ability to prepare for the outbreak. The WHO is under particular strain after the US ceased funding and withdrew from the agency. Pledges have still been made: The UK is providing $26 million, South Africa $2.5 million, the US $23 million, and the UN has allocated $60 from an emergency fund. However, this is well short of the nearly $1 billion mobilised for the 2018-2020 outbreak. Stewart Muhindo, a researcher who studied the 2018-2020 epidemic, which also affected North Kivu and Ituri, said the funding cuts may turn out to be a blessing in disguise. He said the scale of the spending in 2018-2020 created problems and detached the response from local realities. He gave the example of responders using large convoys to transport patients to treatment centres as an example of the disconnect. At the time, communities questioned why a large-scale government and international response materialised for Ebola, but not for years of massacres or preventable diseases such as cholera and malaria. In the previous collaborative episode between Rethinking Humanitarianism and Start Network , Fogbow CEO Brook Jerue questioned why the aid sector was so “infatuated” and critical of his company – a small private American firm delivering aid in high‐conflict contexts like South Sudan and Gaza. In this follow‐up episode, host Tammam Aloudat speaks with Beatrice Lindstrom – co‐author of a recent policy brief on the rise of privatised, militarised, and politicised aid actors – to situate Fogbow within the larger context of these emerging operators, and to examine why their growing "subsumption" of professional humanitarian roles deserves closer scrutiny. Lindstrom, who is also a human rights lawyer and a senior clinical instructor at Harvard Law’s International Human Rights Clinic, warns that we may be sliding towards a future where “aid-for-profit” becomes normalised at the risk of harming affected communities. She draws distinctions between firms like Fogbow and entities such as the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, whose US‐Israeli‐backed activities were linked to Israel’s killing of thousands of aid seekers . Yet, she argues, they share structural features that matter: corporate structures and incentives, close relationships with states that are parties to conflict, and approaches that risk turning aid into an instrument of military and political strategy. A central concern for Lindstrom is the ambiguous nature of these companies, which “seem to be asking to be held to corporate transparency standards rather than humanitarian ones”. That mix, she says, creates “a grey zone of accountability” in which people in crisis – and the public funding much of the response – lack clear information on who is calling the shots, whose interests are being served, and what safeguards exist when those interests clash. Lindstrom links this shift to “massive defunding” of professional aid organisations and a deliberate policy turn by major donors like the United States. This is embracing “a philosophy around aid that is entirely instrumentalised to serve American interests, and where private actors are named as core actors to carry out that plan”. While private actors have long been in the humanitarian space, Lindstrom says the sector is “on the cusp of a broader trend” where aid-for-profit models risk becoming increasingly accepted and entrenched, “and I think that that's exactly why it's so critical that we scrutinise these actors adequately right now, before they are legitimised”. Lindstrom says traditional NGOs also fall short, especially on accountability to affected people, but insists that this cannot be a reason to abandon core principles. “I don't think we're disproportionately focused on for-profit companies here, but rather that this conversation now needs to be applied to these new actors in the same way that it's been applied to nonprofit organisations,” she says. “We all share a responsibility to fight for a model of aid grounded in needs and rights, and kept at arm’s length from politics.” Guests Beatrice Lindstrom, senior clinical instructor at Harvard Law School's International Human Rights Clinic; co-author of "The New Humanitarian Actors: Politicization, Corporatization, and Militarization in the Aid Sector” Read more Rethinking Humanitarianism | The rise of privatised aid: A conversation with Fogbow The New Humanitarian Actors: Politicization, Corporatization, & Militarization in the Aid Sector The problem with emergency aid’s growing reliance on corporations Subscribe on Spotify , Apple , Google , Stitcher , or YouTube , or search “The New Humanitarian” in your favourite podcast app. Got a question or feedback? Email [email protected] or have your say on Twitter using the hashtag #RethinkingHumanitarianism. Transcript | Will aid-for-hire become the new normal? Beatrice Lindstrom They seem to be asking to be held to corporate transparency standards rather than humanitarian ones, and that the funding sources are largely not disclosed. [...] And I think ultimately my concern here is that this combination can create sort of a grey zone of accountability, because they can present themselves as mission-driven when it's convenient, but also as a commercial actor when it's advantageous [...] and in a humanitarian context, that ambiguity matters because people in crisis, and the public that is funding much of this work, they deserve clarity about whose interests are being served, and what safeguards exist when those interests conflict. It was an interesting conversation, and I think we do, we did need to elaborate on that further, didn't we? Christina Bennett Yeah, I think it was really important to put that conversation with Fogbow into context, and I think the conversation with Beatrice has done that. I think she did a really good job of zooming out from the implications of what that conversation might mean for the future of aid. Tammam Aloudat Yeah. Christina Bennett For me, it isn't a question of whether aid can be delivered efficiently. I think the conversation with Fogbow demonstrated that, you know, there are organisations that are able to do things very quickly, very efficiently, very cost effectively, and getting aid on the ground or getting aid to people. But it begs the question: Is the efficient delivery aid enough? And is it,if efficiency comes at the expense of, you know, the principles, the practices, the standards that we have held dear for so long, is it worth it? Tammam Aloudat And as well as the accountability and transparency that we take for granted, and that isn't binding for corporate entities. Is it principled? Is it not having unintended harm? Is it not causing political cost to this very people we're trying to aid? Humanitarian finance Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email GENEVA Norwegian People’s Aid will turn down millions in US government funding due to wide-reaching restrictions on reproductive health and equity, the mine action group announced, in a rare example of a humanitarian organisation publicly rejecting US cash. The decision could affect 40% of NPA’s de-mining budget and 1,700 jobs, and will have “major consequences” for the organisation, NPA said. Few humanitarian groups have spoken publicly about the so-called “global gag rules” since the Trump administration expanded the discriminatory restrictions this year . The regulations, known as the Mexico City policy, handcuff organisations receiving US cash even if potentially banned work is paid for in separate budgets by other donors. Over decades, the US has repeatedly rescinded then reinstated the global gag rule as the government lurches between Democrat and Republican-led administrations. “I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years.” Previous versions have tried to block organisations that receive US health funding from providing or promoting abortion care as part of family planning – even if the money came from other sources. This year, the Trump administration has expanded the rules to cover almost all foreign aid including humanitarian funding, and to target gender identity and diversity, equity, and inclusion. “We see that a more rights-based approach is being challenged globally,” Gry Ballestad, NPA’s director of policy and communications, said in an interview. “And I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years.” The restrictions affecting NPA cover funding from the US State Department’s Office of Weapons Removal and Abatement. Critics say the global gag rules are an attempt to co-opt international aid along US ideological lines. The US made drastic cuts to humanitarian budgets when it dismantled its aid programme last year, which could lead to millions of deaths, a study published in The Lancet estimated. But other governments are also cutting back – leaving the US as a top humanitarian donor that can shape how and where the system works by sheer volume. For example, the US has earmarked some $3.75 billion to UN-run pooled funds – roughly 83% of total funds so far, and $3.6 billion more than the next largest donor. It has also promised hundreds of millions more directly to UN agencies like the World Food Programme and UNICEF, or non-governmental organisations like World Vision . The initial $2 billion to UN pooled funds was signed just before the global gag rule’s new restrictions came into effect. Ballestad spoke to The New Humanitarian about NPA’s decision, its consequences, and what this moment means for the wider humanitarian and development sectors. This interview was edited for length and clarity. The New Humanitarian: Can you describe the decision-making process: What were the considerations? Gry Ballestad: It’s been a difficult decision given the implications, the programmes it affects around the world, the size of the funding, all the people that will be losing their jobs, and the impact on the ground. It’s been a very difficult decision to take. In [2026], the big change for us was that now the requirements are not just for the American funding – not just the mine action programmes funded by the State Department, but it would affect also all our other activities and programmes... This would put limitations on everything we do – not just the American funding. When we started working with the Americans, these were not the requirements we signed on to – actually, quite the opposite. For a long time, it’s been a requirement that we do take into consideration equal opportunities and all these things that are now a problem. We see that now, with the change in the requirements, and looking at our core values and principles, that it’s such a big change that we cannot accept it. Because there’s a change in the regulation, we would basically have to change our core values, our activities – really, who we are. NPA is not just working on mine action. We are the humanitarian solidarity organisation of the labour movement. That’s our origin. Our core values are very much linked to the labour movement. They’re very close to us still. Basically, we would have to change who we are. We would have to change our core values. We have a big programme in Norway that’s working on search-and-rescue activities, but also integration activities. For example, today we had the launch of our new anti-racism guidelines for our members, and other organisations, on how to work on anti-racism. We have local chapters all over the country, and they are very much involved in integration and anti-racism activities. We couldn’t do that. It would affect what we do also in Norway together with our partners around the world. And it’s not something we can accept. It’s beyond the American funding. It would affect who we are, how we operate. Of course, we can’t change our identity and all of our activities because one of our donors changed their requirements. The New Humanitarian: I think what people might not understand is how far the global gag rule reaches. Ballestad: It’s very broad. For us, it’s very much about who we are. What are the core values of an organisation like NPA? The first paragraph of our principles ... says “Norwegian People’s Aid’s values are based on equal rights for all regardless of gender, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, functional ability, and social status. Norwegian People's Aid is an anti-racist organisation.” That’s the first paragraph. So already there, we’re in trouble. What’s the game-changer this time: The [US] requirements that came out in [2025] were similar, but they were only for American-funded activities. This time, it would cover all of what we do. You can’t compensate for what you can’t do with American funding with other funding. It would affect who we are, how we operate. Of course, we can’t change our identity and all of our activities because one of our donors changed their requirements. It’s basically about our political freedom. The New Humanitarian: Many mine action programmes have focused on recruiting women as de-miners. Is something like that – the US would consider that to be non-compliant? Ballestad: Yes. When we advertise, for example, sometimes we encourage women to apply so that we can have more of a gender balance in, for example, our management positions. This, we wouldn’t be allowed to do. And we do that for everything. That’s part of our HR policies. There’s a lot of levels that we would have to change. We can’t accept it. Of course, Americans set their requirements for their funding. But we have to assess if this is something we can accept to remain true to our foundational values. The New Humanitarian: Looking at the entire aid sector, why do you think it’s important that NPA made this decision? What’s the significance of it? Ballestad: In the bigger picture, we see that a more rights-based approach is being challenged globally. And I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years. It costs, if you stand up for rights. And I think it’s the time to do so. It’s a slippery slope... Currently, these are the rights we’re discussing. You don’t know what’s next. When do you put your foot down? Edited by Andrew Gully. Read the first report here . MAIDUGURI, Nigeria Mamman Nur, the senior cleric of Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), had tried to escape detention by his own comrades twice before – he knew this failed third attempt was likely his death sentence. The influential ideologue had been a leading figure in Nigeria’s insurgent jihadist movement for more than two decades. He had been one of the closest aides to Boko Haram’s deceased founder, Mohammed Yusuf, was a key link to Islamic State-Central, and for a time was popularly thought of as ISWAP’s leader. But the tall, charismatic teacher was now undone. He had been accused of secret contact with the Nigerian government through an initiative known as the “Swiss process”, which was exploring a path to dialogue and regarded Nur as a possible interlocutor . To ISWAP’s governing Shura council, this was treason. With the blessing of IS-Central, Nur was detained while the council debated what to do. In September 2018, he was sentenced to death and publicly shot by the head of the amniya , ISWAP’s secret police. Nur’s fate exposed the central problem facing any attempt to negotiate with Nigeria’s jihadists: Can a movement that treats dialogue as treason ever be persuaded to make peace? Nearly eight years later, a reported ceasefire between the government and Boko Haram suggests that, however tentatively, the answer may be changing. Can you make peace with jihadists? After 17 years of war and close to 350,000 indirect civilian deaths , the conflict in Nigeria’s northeast is stalemated. Yet behind the scenes there has been a long if faltering attempt by the Nigerian government to find a negotiated breakthrough to the jihadist insurgency. The idea of negotiations with “Boko Haram” – officially Jama’at Ahl al Sunna li Da’wa wal Jihad (JAS) – and ISWAP, its offshoot and rival, sharply divides Nigeria. The government officially says there can be no talks with groups legally proscribed as terrorist organisations, even though a three-month ceasefire with JAS, agreed in June, seems to be holding . The New Humanitarian has spoken to security officials, diplomats, mediators, and former jihadist fighters – protecting their anonymity so they could speak freely – to explore the potential of that dialogue process. Is there a path to a sustainable peace with extremist groups that reject the legitimacy of the Nigerian state, its secular constitution, and world view? “Both sides believe a settlement is possible,” a diplomat with knowledge of the chronology of the dialogue process told The New Humanitarian. “For all parties, a non-kinetic [military] approach is intellectually acceptable.” Military operations alone rarely resolves insurgencies. Political settlements, where they are possible, are more likely to produce lasting peace. But governments tend to exceptionalise jihadist groups and publicly shun the idea of dialogue with people typically characterised as irredeemably violent. These groups’ perceived maximalist ideological demands are seen as obstacles to peace – the spiritual and sacred regarded as incompatible with the give and take of political bargaining. Yet Islamist ideology is not monolithic . Extremist groups are political actors that shape and are shaped by their environments. Supposed “red lines” over political demands can also fade over time. In Egypt, Gama’a al Islamiya carried out armed attacks for two decades before it renounced violence and stood in elections in 2011. And more recently, in Syria, Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham transformed from an al-Qaeda franchise into the dominant force behind a transitional government. However, the cell-like structures of jihadist groups, legal prohibitions, histories of distrust, and the difficulty of building domestic political consensus all weigh on the timing and incentives for peace talks. Negotiations demand patience, political will, and good intelligence networks, said the diplomat. Nigeria has struggled on all three fronts. Successive governments have also avoided confronting the grievances driving the northeastern conflict or properly understanding their opponents. The traditional establishment approach has been to “settle” troublemakers, buying them off with money and positions. But JAS and ISWAP have been different: ideological foes not seeking a financial reward or patronage. “Peace can be possible, but it needs trust and sincerity,” a former ISWAP commander who surrendered to the authorities last year, told The New Humanitarian. “The problem is that up until now, nobody has sat with [JAS/ISWAP] to understand them. A close observer of the Nigerian conflict was more sceptical. “The record shows that jihadist groups, like other insurgent groups, can engage in negotiations, at least preliminary or limited ones, when they are under pressure,” he noted. However, there are fewer examples of longer-term political solutions. Talking about talks The insurgency, which began in northeastern Maiduguri in 2009, was still growing when President Goodluck Jonathan was elected two years later. A southern Christian, his poll victory sparked riots in several predominantly Muslim northern cities in a controversy over whether he should have stood. For some in his administration it was proof of a conspiracy : that JAS was manufactured by aggrieved northern elites to undermine Jonathan’s rule. In the early days of the conflict, mediation efforts were largely privately led. Former president Olusegun Obasanjo made the first attempt in 2011, followed by Sheikh Ibrahim Datti Ahmad, the respected president of the National Supreme Council of Sharia. Both ended almost as soon as they had begun – with each side blaming the other. Demands by JAS were basic: the release of detained wives and colleagues, the rebuilding of homes and buildings destroyed by the security forces in Maiduguri, the payment of compensation to families of members killed, and the prosecution of the policemen responsible for the assassination of Yusuf, the movement’s founder. They have not included larger ideological goals. Splits and rivalries: A timeline of Boko Haram/ISWAP discord Boko Haram began as an ultra-conservative religious movement in the early 2000s in Maiduguri under a young cleric, Mohammed Yusuf. It tapped into a radical zeitgeist that appealed across classes – condemning so-called “Western values” and celebrating 500 years of Islamic learning and empire in Nigeria’s northeast. Initially, Yusuf resisted calling for jihad, but as tensions with the authorities increased, he launched an urban insurrection in July 2009. It was quickly crushed, and Yusuf was extrajudicially killed by the police. Abubakar Shekau, his deputy, took over as imam. A wave of bombings, kidnappings, and the overrunning of towns had the army on the backfoot, and rural Borno emptied as people were displaced from their homes. Shekau declared allegiance to so-called Islamic State in 2015 and the group was renamed Islamic State of West Africa Province (ISWAP). In 2016, ISWAP split. Dissident commanders led by Abu Musa al-Barnawi and cleric Mamman Nur accused Shekau of despotism and condemned his use of “takfir” – the death penalty for infidels – against rural civilians. Bitter factional fighting followed, but the dissidents managed to establish themselves in the Lake Chad region and win the blessing of IS-Central. https://astana.osce.org/news/programme-o.body: News News Item OSCE supports evidence-based basin planning through stakeholder consultations and data verification in Kazakhstan Issued on: 4 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Astana From 26 July to 4 August 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Astana, in partnership with the Information and Analytical Center for Water Resources under the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, supported a series of consultations with basin inspections and other water-sector stakeholders in the Aral-Syrdarya, Zhaiyk-Caspian and Yertis basins. The consultations formed part of Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to develop basin plans and a General Plan for integrated water resources management based on accurate, up-to-date and jointly verified data. The consultations brought together more than 100 representatives of basin inspections, branches of the Republican State Enterprise (RSE) “Kazvodkhoz” and RSE “Kazhydromet”, local executive bodies, water-user organizations, and scientific and research institutions. Conducted by a team of three water specialists (two women and one man), the meetings took place from 26 to 29 July in Kyzylorda, from 30 to 31 July in Aktau, and from 2 to 4 August in Semey and Oskemen. Participants worked to verify baseline data, align projected water balances with local investment and development plans, and identify measures for inclusion in the basin plans. The consultations combined technical review with field observation. Participants examined water-use limits, the accuracy of water accounting and metering, the condition of hydraulic infrastructure and irrigation canals, transportation losses, and the fulfilment of transboundary commitments. Discussions also addressed the functioning of basin councils, the participation of water users and the public, and the availability and quality of data required for basin planning. Field visits to key water infrastructure and water-use facilities enabled participants to connect the planning process with conditions on the ground. Working directly with the expert team, representatives of the basin inspections also reconciled discrepancies between primary reporting data and previously prepared analytical materials. This included correcting data on water-supply sources and transboundary inflows in the three basins, strengthening the basis for calculating water balances under current and future demand scenarios. The consultations also highlighted priorities for continued investment in canal rehabilitation, water-saving technologies and monitoring networks. By bringing together national authorities, basin inspections, water users and other stakeholders to verify data and jointly identify priorities, the consultations strengthened the evidentiary basis for Kazakhstan’s basin plans and General Plan for integrated water resources management. The initiative supports the country’s long-term efforts to strengthen water security, transboundary co-operation and sustainable water governance, in line with OSCE commitments and international good practices.
